title: Why Being An Authoritarian Teacher Is A Big Mistake
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes firm classroom management from authoritarianism, arguing students crave clear boundaries but rebel privately against rules imposed as arbitrary decrees. He defines authoritarian teaching as a style marked by dominance, where rules function as executive orders handed down without explanation, and argues this approach breeds resentment even when it produces surface compliance. His central solution is to attach a clear, describable 'why' to every rule, consequence, policy, and routine — if a teacher cannot explain the benefit to students, he argues, the policy shouldn't exist. He frames a stated why as serving multiple purposes: it makes the same firm enforcement feel legitimate rather than dictatorial, it protects teachers against pushback from parents and administrators, and it forces teachers to genuinely think through what is best for students rather than enforcing rules out of habit or convenience. The piece closes by reframing all classroom rules as existing entirely for students' benefit, not the teacher's convenience.
points: Firm boundaries are something students crave, but rules imposed as arbitrary decrees without explanation breed private resentment and rebellion.
Authoritarianism is defined as a classroom management style marked by dominance, where rules function as unquestionable executive orders.
Every rule, consequence, and routine should have a clear, describable benefit to students that the teacher is ready to explain — never 'because I said so.'
Explaining the 'why' behind rules protects teachers from pushback by parents and administrators, since a stated benefit is hard to argue against.
Thinking through and stating the 'why' forces teachers to confirm that every classroom policy genuinely serves students, not just the teacher's convenience.
quotes: Kids don’t misbehave because they don’t want discipline. They misbehave because they do.
If the discipline is meted out by an authoritarian, it will be met with private resentment and rebellion—especially among your most difficult students.
Rules are a form of executive order. They come down via royal decree and are not to be questioned. Just followed without complaint.
Everything you do, from rules and consequences to policies and routines, must have a compelling reason why you’re doing it .
Every classroom management policy must have a why that students understand. And you must be ready to explain it to them. “Because I said so” doesn’t cut it.
They’re for them and wholly and completely for their benefit.
